This atlas collects the results of a corpus-wide search for arithmetic links between khipus in the open data of the Open Khipu Repository and the Khipu Field Guide, with two khipus we transcribed from record-sheet scans. Every detector was first run on relations already published, and every result was compared with structure-preserving baselines.

We ran arithmetic detectors over about 700 digitized khipus and compared every hit with a baseline that keeps the khipus' structure. What survives is a set of copies and excerpts. Some keep only the totals of an account, some only its details, some split one account over two khipus or join two accounts on one. We found no summary khipu built from other surviving khipus.

We ran arithmetic detectors over about 700 digitized khipus and kept only the matches that stand far above a baseline that keeps the khipus' structure. Read as records, what survives looks like copies and excerpts of accounts: some keep only the totals, some only the details, some split one account over two khipus or join two on one. The numbers establish the matches; reading them as copies is an interpretation, and each finding sets out the two separately.

mixed.start-what:
What is a khipu?

A khipu (also spelled quipu, from the Quechua word for “knot”) is a set of knotted cords that people in the Andes used to keep records. Most surviving khipus come from the Inka empire, which ruled the Andes from Ecuador to Chile in the fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, until the Spanish conquest of 1532. Some are older, from the Wari state (about AD 600–1000). Khipus were made of cotton or camelid fibre, often dyed, and could hold from a handful to more than a thousand cords.

Spanish chroniclers describe specialists, the khipukamayuq, who kept khipus of the census, of tribute and of the contents of storehouses, and who “read” them aloud to officials. Some villages in Peru still kept khipus as community records in the twentieth century.
mixed.start-numbers:
How numbers were knotted

Many khipus record numbers in a decimal system that has been understood since 1912 (L. L. Locke). Each hanging cord carries one number. Position along the cord gives the place value: knots nearest the main cord are the highest place (thousands, hundreds), knots farthest from it are the units. An empty position means zero.
mixed.start-legend: F primary cord, from which the others hang. A reads 251: two single knots in the hundreds, five in the tens, a figure-eight knot for one unit. B reads 73: seven single knots in the tens and a long knot of three turns. C reads 304: the tens position is empty, so it is zero; the units are a long knot of four turns. E is a subsidiary, a cord tied to another cord (here 5). D is a top cord, rising above the primary cord; it carries 628, the sum of A, B and C. Sums like this, inside one khipu, are how much of khipu arithmetic was discovered.
mixed.start-where:
Where do they come from?

Roughly a thousand khipus survive in museums around the world. Most come from burials on the dry Pacific coast of Peru and northern Chile, where the desert preserved the fibre. Many were dug up in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, often by grave robbers (huaqueros), and sold to collectors and museums in Lima, Berlin, New York and elsewhere. As a result, the place recorded for a khipu is often only what a dealer said. About 700 khipus have been recorded cord by cord and are openly available as data; this atlas uses them.
mixed.start-known:
What we know, and what we don't

We can read the numbers on most khipus, and many khipus add up: one cord often holds the sum of a group of others. Khipus from an Inka storehouse at Inkawasi record deliveries of produce with a fixed deduction taken from each. What the numbers counted — people, llamas, bags of maize — is usually unknown, because the labels were kept by colours, cord order and the memory of the reader, not in writing. Whether some khipus also recorded words or stories is still debated. Only a handful of khipus have been matched to Spanish written records, such as khipus from the Santa valley and a colonial census (Medrano 2021).
mixed.start-project:
What this project does

Most studies look inside one khipu at a time. We looked for numbers shared between different khipus: one khipu that copies another, or one that holds the totals of another. Such links show how accountants handled several records of the same business — who kept the details and who kept the totals. With a computer we compared every khipu in the open data with every other one.

Because the corpus is large, some coincidences are bound to happen. So every link is tested against chance: we run the same search with the numbers slightly shifted, which keeps everything else the same, and count how many matches appear by accident. A link is reported only if it stands far above that level. Weaker patterns are labelled “suggestive”, and the searches that found nothing are listed under Negative results.
mixed.start-use:
How to use the atlas

  • Overview — the main results on one page.
  • Map — where the khipus were found; red arcs join places with linked khipus. Switch to 3D relief to see the coast and the Andes.
  • Links — a network of the khipus that are linked to each other.
  • Catalogue — every khipu, with its museum, find-place, a 3D model and its cord values. Type a number such as AS143 or UR212 in the search box at the top.
  • Findings — one page per result, with the evidence and the scripts that reproduce it.
  • Tools — search for a sequence of numbers across all khipus, or compare two khipus.
  • Timeline, Statistics, On the object (what only a visit to the museum can settle), Sources.
mixed.start-glossary:
Words used on this site

Primary cord
the main cord from which the others hang.
Pendant
a cord hanging from the primary cord; it usually carries one number.
Subsidiary
a cord tied to another cord rather than to the primary cord.
Top cord
a cord rising above the primary cord, often holding a sum.
Group
pendants set close together, separated from the next group by a space; groups often have the same structure.
Single, long and figure-eight knots
single knots count tens, hundreds and higher places; a long knot (2–9 turns) or a figure-eight knot (one) gives the units.
AS, UR, KH, MM…
catalogue numbers. AS numbers were given by Marcia and Robert Ascher, UR numbers by Gary Urton, KH numbers by the Khipu Field Guide; one khipu can have several. Museum numbers such as VA 42508 belong to the museums.
OKR, KFG
the Open Khipu Repository and the Khipu Field Guide, the two open databases of khipu recordings used here.
Copy, extract
a khipu that repeats the values of another, completely or in part.
Baseline
how many matches the same search finds by chance; a result counts only if it is far above it.
mixed.start-read:
To read further

Gary Urton, Inka History in Knots (2017); Marcia and Robert Ascher, Code of the Quipu (1981; the Databook is online at Cornell); Frank Salomon, The Cord Keepers (2004), on khipus kept in a Peruvian village. Our full results are in the preprint.
mixed.sure:
How sure are we?

The detectors compare every khipu with every other, so some unusual matches are bound to turn up by chance. The baselines therefore repeat the whole search, not a single comparison: the same scan run with all target numbers shifted by a few units shows how many matches the number of comparisons alone produces. The Pachacamac–Huacho copy is the strongest pair of its scan apart from second recordings of one object and copies already known.

Some tests were made after a pattern had been noticed: the pairing of units on the Basel fragments, the fourteen-unit frame, the empty slots of UR255, and the place-set deduction and stream alignment of UR269. Their p-values describe a pattern once seen, not the chance of finding some pattern somewhere; where we could, we tested the pattern again without the khipus that suggested it, or searched the whole corpus for it (UR269's structure occurs nowhere else). Each finding separates what the numbers show from how we read them. Rerun on the Khipu Field Guide release of October 2026, which revises the readings of about 200 khipus, every result holds; only the exact counts move a little.
mixed.repo: Scripts, the full report and the study log are in the repository github.com/VladimirMoor/khipu-links; the paper is the preprint (PDF, version 4). Cord data come from the OKR (MIT licence) and the KFG; please cite them when you use the values.

basel.title: Two Pachacamac accounts joined on a Huacho khipu
basel.summary: Six fragments sewn on the Basel cloth IVc.366.03 (dug near Huacho, bought 1910) repeat runs of two Berlin khipus labelled Pachacamac: UR212 (37 of 195 pendants) and AS131 (25 of 146). UR212 and AS131 each have 14 main groups, divided 7 + 7 at the same point. Every fragment that carries both khipus pairs the same unit (units 1, 4 and 14), so the Huacho khipu set the two halves of one 14-unit account side by side, 14 + 10 cords per unit.
evidence: Other khipus with ≥ 100 pendants match at most 4 cords (median 0).
Same unit in 3 of 3 fragments: p ≈ (1/14)² ≈ 0.005.
Where Berlin leaves a colour-marked cord knotless, the Basel copy carries a value (3 of 3); other knotless cords stay knotless.
Unit totals of UR212 and AS131 are not correlated (ρ = 0.19): different categories of the same units.

levels.numbers: Six fragments repeat 37 cords of UR212 and 25 of AS131; other khipus with at least 100 pendants match at most 4. In each of the 3 fragments that carry both, they pair the same unit (p ≈ 0.005, computed after the pairing was noticed).
levels.structure: Both Berlin khipus have 14 units divided 7 + 7 at the same point; their unit totals are uncorrelated, so they record different categories of the same units.
levels.reading: Two halves of one fourteen-unit account set side by side on a khipu from Huacho. The fragments were sewn onto a cloth in 1924, so their order on the cloth says nothing.

frame14.title: A 14-unit frame in Gretzer's Berlin batch
frame14.summary: Fourteen main groups are rare (1.6% of khipus outside the Berlin 'Pachacamac' batch) but occur on 4 of 23 khipus of that batch: UR212, AS131, AS170 and UR199. The Berlin catalogue describes one more that is not digitized, VA 42537 (14 × 9); two other records with this frame, VA 42513 (14 × 13 pendants) and VA 42532 (7 × A, 7 × B, 7 × A, 7 × B), are UR212 and UR199 themselves, as the KFG release of October 2026 numbers them. AS131, UR212 and AS170 split their units 7 + 7 at the same place, each marked differently: a larger space, a single knotless cord, a marker.
evidence: Binomial P ≈ 0.0005 with all four; P ≈ 0.04 without the two khipus that prompted the question.
Across 109 OKR khipus with an even number of main groups, the largest space falls in the middle 12.9 times (13.0 expected): equal halves are not a general habit.

levels.numbers: 4 of the 23 khipus of the batch have 14 main groups, against 1.6% elsewhere (P ≈ 0.0005; P ≈ 0.04 without the two khipus that prompted the question).
levels.structure: Three of them divide their units 7 + 7, each marked differently; one undigitized khipu of the batch, VA 42537, is described with 14 groups.
levels.reading: Suggestive only: a shared fourteen-unit frame in one archive. What the units were is unknown.

berlin.title: One allocation on three Ica khipus (Berlin, 1907)
berlin.summary: AS143 group 4 equals AS149 groups 1 + 2 in all five positions (17436 = 8653 + 8783, 41883 = 20640 + 21243, …). All shares have the same composition (22.4 : 10.4 : 54.4 : 12.8 %); in ninths of the AS143 total the shares are 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1. The lot 1430, 670, 3410, 820 recurs on AS179.
evidence: The only exact cross-khipu vector sum in the corpus (offset baseline 0–2, small values only).
Two 2/9 shares of AS143 are equal within 1 (41062 and 41061) with a substitution between goods (p ≈ 0.005).

A second, different composition from the same Berlin Ica batch: UR1120 (AS120, VA47083) has four rows of eight cords whose totals (146,087, 49,783, 62,850, 33,455) are divided by the same shares, about 17.6 / 0.7 / 29.3 / 1.3 / 13.2 / 3.8 / 4.5 / 29.7% (rows 1 and 2 proportional within 1–2%: 25,691 / 8,731 = 2.94, 43,372 / 14,701 = 2.95). A corpus-wide search for proportional groups finds only UR1120, AS143 (UR1143) and the Inkawasi nine-part tables.

levels.numbers: AS143 group 4 = AS149 groups 1 + 2 in all five positions: the only exact sum between two khipus in a scan of the whole corpus; the same scan with the numbers shifted by 1–7 finds 0–2, all on small values.
levels.structure: Every share has the same four-part composition; the shares are 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 1 ninths of the AS143 total; a standard lot of AS149 recurs on AS179.
levels.reading: One quantity apportioned to five recipients and recorded at three levels on three khipus. What was shared, and among whom, is unknown.

ica109.title: A private khipu holds the section totals of Berlin AS109 (Ica)
ica109.summary: KH0697 (AK002), a khipu in a private collection, formerly in the Maiman Collection in Tel Aviv, without a recorded provenance, has groups that equal the totals of whole sections of AS109, a Berlin khipu from Ica of Gretzer's 1907 batch. Its groups 7 and 8, [755, 1501, 1100, 330, 1136], equal the sum of AS109 groups 33–41 in all five positions; the sum of groups 12–20 differs by one knot (1126); group 4, [766, 1572, 1120, 520, 1137], matches the sum of groups 2–10 in three positions and has 120 moved between the last two (640 + 1017 = 520 + 1137). Its groups 9–15 match nothing in the corpus. KH0697 was first published in the Khipu Field Guide release of October 2026.
evidence: 14 matches of four or five positions, all with AS109, against 0 in 40 searches with the target values shifted by ±1…±20; AK001, AK003 and BA001 from the same collection match nothing.
The match with groups 33–41 also holds in the 2023 data of AS109.

levels.numbers: Group 7 (= group 8) of KH0697 equals the sum of nine groups of AS109 in all five positions; 14 matches of four or more positions with AS109 against 0 in 40 shifted-value searches over the whole corpus.
levels.structure: Groups 4–8 of KH0697 follow the totals of four sections of AS109: one exactly, one to a knot, one with 120 moved between two positions, as on AS143; groups 9–15 have no counterpart in the corpus.
levels.reading: Either KH0697 keeps the section totals of AS109 and of other, lost khipus, or both apply one standard quota per unit (755, 1501, 1100, 330, 1136). Either way the two belong to one accounting circle, so KH0697 probably comes from the same find at Ica as the Berlin batch.

huacho1.title: Pachacamac → Huacho: the details without the totals
huacho1.summary: The spliced Huacho khipus UR233 + UR232 (Berlin VA 63038b, Gaffron) repeat parts 1 and 3 of AS175 (VA 42518, Gretzer) group by group, leave out part 2 (the sums of part 3) and add one knotless pendant to every group.
evidence: z = 6.4 and 19.5 against other offsets; group-order permutation p ≤ 0.003.
Different objects: cords per group, lengths and subsidiaries differ.

levels.numbers: Group-by-group alignment z = 6.4 (UR233) and 19.5 (UR232) against all other offsets; no permutation of group order reaches it (p ≤ 0.003). In the scan of all pairs it is the strongest pair that is neither a second recording of one object nor a copy already known.
levels.structure: UR233 repeats part 1 of AS175 and UR232 part 3, group for group; part 2, the sums of part 3, is absent; every group gains one empty pendant; the copy fits the part-2 sums better than the original (8 of 15 against 5).
levels.reading: A copy of the details made without the totals. When it was made, by whom, and how it reached Huacho is unknown; a radiocarbon date of VA63038 would show whether it is Inka or colonial.

as118.title: AS118 links two other Pachacamac khipus
as118.summary: Groups 2–3 of AS118 repeat groups 2–3 of UR218 cord for cord, knot counts included. The five subsidiaries of its first, knotless pendant follow the group totals of AS125: 14658 exact, 8565 if one cord the Aschers left unread is 3111.
evidence: Among 696 khipus only AS125 matches more than one of the five values; none on the offset baseline.

levels.numbers: Groups 2–3 equal those of UR218 cord for cord, knot counts included. Of the five subsidiary values, one equals a group total of AS125 exactly and two more do if two cords of AS125 read as 3111 and 2298; among 696 khipus only AS125 (and its second recording) matches more than one.
levels.structure: An extract of one khipu and the totals of another, kept on a cord that was attached before it was knotted.
levels.reading: A khipu that links two other records. It rests partly on two readings that only the object can settle (AS125 group 4 cord 1, group 3 cord 1).

ur269.title: Inkawasi UR269: five supply streams, each with its own deduction
ur269.summary: In blocks of five records [gross, net, deduction] the deduction is 47, 46, 46, 44, 25 by place, whatever the deposit size. The place-1 records are deliveries of the stream recorded in full on UR275 (deduction 47 throughout) and its copy UR266: 5 of 10 place-1 records reappear on UR275, at one fixed offset (block b of UR269 = entry b + 15 of UR275), while places 2–5 are found on no other khipu. Each block is one round of five streams in a fixed order, each stream with its own fixed deduction. Urton & Chu (2015, 2018, 2019) list UR269 as having no repeating value. The five place deductions add up to 208, the fixed deduction of UR268, and UR268 follows UR275 record by record: its 16 four-cord rows rise and fall with the 16 four-cord rows of UR275, in the same order, 3 to 6 times larger (Spearman 0.83, p ≈ 0.0002) — UR268 records whole rounds of the five streams, UR275 the first stream.
evidence: 33 of 43 deductions equal their place value; 17 when records are shuffled within blocks (p ≈ 0.0005).
Place 1 on UR275: 5 of 10 records (0.5 expected); places 2–4: 0, 1, 1. All five at one offset; 5,000 permutations of block order reach at most 4 (p ≈ 0.0002).
UR269 keeps the arithmetic where UR275 slips: 1827 = 1780 + 47 on UR269, 1825 on UR275.
No other Inkawasi khipu shows a place dependence (all p > 0.8).

UR268 against UR275, four-cord rows in order: Spearman 0.83 (16 rows; ratio 2.8–5.9, median 4.4 ≈ 208/47); the same at other offsets ≤ 0.39; three-cord rows do not follow (−0.13). Three UR268 rows lie within 3–12 of UR269 round totals (9332 / 9335, 10,385 / 10,379, 8527 / 8515).

levels.numbers: The deduction equals the value of its place in 33 of 43 records (17 when records are shuffled within blocks; p ≈ 0.0005). The place-1 records reappear on UR275 at one offset (5 matches; at most 4 in 5,000 permutations of block order; p ≈ 0.0002). Both patterns were found by exploring the Inkawasi khipus; a search of the whole corpus finds the place-set deduction nowhere else.
levels.structure: Blocks of five records, each place with its own fixed deduction; stream 1 is recorded in full, in the same sequence, on UR275.
levels.reading: Five supply streams delivered in rounds, each with its own deduction. What the streams were (producers, fields, villages) is unknown.

inkawasi.title: Inkawasi: empty slots, totals-only copies, product labels
inkawasi.summary: On UR255 the net pendant is empty in the first 12 deposits and filled with the values of UR267A in 5 of the last 6. The bundle UR273A + UR273B records only the deposit totals of UR274A + UR274B: 4 and 6 shared totals (0.3 and 0.5 expected), in the same order on both. Copies lie in a different bundle from their counterparts. A red tassel at the start of the primary cord occurs only on peanut khipus (2 of 4 against 0 of 25).
evidence: Split this clean under random placement: about 1 in 3,900.
UR273B ~ UR274B: Poisson p ≈ 10⁻⁵.
UR273A ~ UR274A: 891, 453, 448, 448 in the same order (p ≈ 3 × 10⁻⁴); UR273B ~ UR274B: six totals in the same order (p ≈ 10⁻⁵).

levels.numbers: UR255 leaves the net pendant empty in its first 12 deposits and fills it in 5 of the last 6 (about 1 in 3,900 by chance); UR273A/B share 4 and 6 totals with UR274A/B against 0.3 and 0.5 expected, in the same order.
levels.structure: Each copy lies in a different bundle from its counterpart; the totals-only bundle keeps the order of the full one.
levels.reading: Copies made or completed at different times, and totals kept apart from the details. Why the slots were left empty is not known.

as003.title: AS003: a record of the totals only
as003.summary: AS003 (Heye 17/8827) repeats the summary part of AS215 (Hood Museum, Nazca): six values that are sums over the four groups of its other part, and the top cord 76 that totals them. It is a second totals-only record, after UR273B at Inkawasi.
evidence: The Aschers' AS215 entry (Databook pp. 127–132) describes the summary but does not mention AS003.

levels.numbers: The six values and their total 76 equal the summary part of AS215, in reverse cord order.
levels.structure: A seven-cord khipu that holds only the totals of another khipu's summary.
levels.reading: A totals-only record. The provenance of AS003 is unknown, so where and why it was made cannot be said.

folded.title: Folded copies
folded.summary: In two independent cases a separate cord in one copy is a subsidiary in the other: UR270 → UR278 at Inkawasi and UR053C → UR053B in the Waterfall set. The packing rule is ours; the near-duplication of B and C was noted by Chirinos.
evidence: UR053B/C: 35 fields match against at most 18 in 2,000 shuffles.

levels.numbers: UR053C → UR053B: 35 fields agree against at most 18 in 2,000 shuffles of the C records; UR270 → UR278: 15 consecutive values.
levels.structure: A cord that stands alone in one copy is a subsidiary in the other, in two independent pairs.
levels.reading: Copies keep the values but not necessarily the cord hierarchy.

known.title: Known copies recovered
known.summary: The detectors find, without being told, the copies already published: Lima → Gothenburg (KH0049 → UR122, one branch of the account), Lima ↔ Paris (HP055 ~ AS084), AS114/AS123 (Urton 2005), Puruchuco UR066 ~ UR067, AS069/AS070 (Thompson 2024), and duplicate recordings of one object.

levels.numbers: The detectors find these published copies without being told where to look.
levels.structure: Copies of one branch of an account, matching pairs and duplicate recordings, as published.
levels.reading: A check of the method, not a new result.

dumbarton.title: Two Dumbarton Oaks khipus transcribed
dumbarton.summary: UR297 (438 pendants, 623 cords) and UR298 (203 pendants, 285 cords), given by Bill Conklin, exist in the OKR only as scans of Urton's handwritten sheets. We transcribed all 65 pages. 74 of the 78 group totals Urton noted on the sheets equal ours. UR297 has 41 groups, mostly ten cords plus one summary cord pulled up like a top cord. Neither khipu is linked to any other.

levels.numbers: 74 of the 78 group totals that Urton noted on his record sheets equal our transcription.
levels.structure: UR297: 41 groups, mostly ten cords plus one summary cord raised like a top cord.
levels.reading: New data. Neither khipu is linked to any other in the corpus.

inkawasi_archive.title: Inkawasi: how the storehouse kept its books
inkawasi_archive.summary: The 52 khipus from the Inka storehouse at Inkawasi (Cañete valley) read as one bookkeeping system on three levels. Tables split each delivery into nine parts (UR278, UR270); their group totals are the gross deliveries entered, in the same order, in the ledgers (UR275 and its copy UR266; UR274B). Each ledger records gross, net and a fixed deduction of its own: 15 and 10 on the two chili ledgers, 47 on the peanut ledger UR275, 47, 46, 46, 44 and 25 by place on UR269, 208 on UR268. Copies keep their ledger's deduction and were stored elsewhere: the chili ledgers in sector A, their copies in sector C. Totals-only records lie next to their full ledgers (layers 14 and 15 of unit 20N). No surviving khipu holds the totals of the others. The fixed deduction was described by Urton and Chu (2015, 2019); the nine-part tables and the layout of the archive as a whole are, as far as we know, new.
evidence: Laid in order against the ledgers' gross deliveries, the nine-cord group totals of UR278 give 10 equal and 4 one knot apart on UR266 (7 and 4 on UR275), those of UR270 4 equal and 1 one knot apart on UR274B; with the ledger values shifted by 1–10 the same alignment finds at most 2. A search of every pair of Inkawasi khipus for such ordered totals finds only these and the known totals-only bundles.

The nine columns keep their order of size from delivery to delivery (Spearman 0.59 between consecutive rows of UR278 and 0.64 on UR270, against 0 when values are shuffled within rows), and both tables rank them alike (0.80, p = 0.007): the same nine suppliers, each giving about a ninth.

Gross = net + deduction in 15 of 25 groups of three on UR267A (deduction 15), 12 of 14 on UR267B (10) and 7 of 9 on UR275 (47); with the values shuffled within each khipu, 0.3 or fewer are expected. Each copy keeps its ledger's deduction: UR255 15, UR256 10, UR266 47.
The large values of UR257 (up to 98,718) match totals of other Inkawasi khipus no more often than shifted values do (3 of 10 against 2.7).

levels.numbers: Nine-part tables whose group totals are the gross deliveries of the ledgers, in order; groups of three that add up (gross = net + deduction) with one deduction per ledger; each copy has the same deduction as its ledger.
levels.structure: Three levels — parts, deliveries, totals — on different khipus; copies of the chili ledgers in another sector, the totals-only bundle next to its full one.
levels.reading: Each delivery made up of nine contributions from the same nine suppliers; separate ledgers for each product and supply stream, each with its own fixed levy; copies kept at a second place, perhaps for checking; summaries kept elsewhere or lost.

as104.title: AS104 keeps the group heads of UR234, including one lost to a broken cord
as104.summary: UR234 (Berlin VA 66837, find-place not recorded; 98 pendants) has ten groups of eight, each headed by a larger cord (2007, 2080, 3012, 2247, 2578, —, 3419, 3159, 1407, —), and two short groups that repeat a list rounded (2500, 2010, 3000, 3159, 1407; 2000, 2086, 2300, 1385, 0 in the KFG reading). AS104 (Berlin VA 42527, Gretzer, labelled Pachacamac; 21 pendants) holds the same list in full: its groups 2 and 3 are the heads of groups 1–9 (3102 for 3012), and its group 4 (2178, 2085, 2329, 1385, 1501) matches the second rounded group. The head of group 6 on UR234 is broken off at 6.5 cm; AS104 has 2016 in that place, and the rounded list 2010 (as the KFG release of October 2026 reads it; the OKR reads 2100). The pair came out of the scan of all pairs of khipus for shared rare values.
evidence: 7 shared rare values (≥ 100, not multiples of 10) against 0.10–0.15 expected from shifted values; the pair passes a Bonferroni threshold over all 286,146 pairs of khipus.
The seven values stand in the same order on both khipus; on UR234 they are the first cords of groups 1, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 9 and a cord of the second rounded group.
The head cords of groups 6 and 10 of UR234 are broken (6.5 and 8 cm, no knots).

levels.numbers: Seven rare values in the same order, far above the shifted baseline; near values (3102/3012, 2085/2086, 2329/2300) fill most of the rest.
levels.structure: On UR234 the values are the heads of its groups and two short groups after them; on AS104 they make up three of its four groups.
levels.reading: AS104 looks like a fair copy of UR234's summary: the heads in full, with the place lost on UR234 still filled. Group 1 of AS104 (18,379–37,076) is not explained by UR234; UR234's find-place is unknown.

copies.title: Copies keep what broke off, and differ by single knots
copies.summary: Where one khipu of a linked pair has a broken cord recorded as 0, the other khipu nearly always has a value in that place: 18 of 21 such cords, against 10 of 29 zeros on intact cords. A zero on a broken cord is a lost value, not a zero, and the copy gives it back (for example 142, 223 and 191 on UR255 from UR267A; 1545 and 1442 on UR266 from UR275; 830 and 3818 on UR122 from KH0049). Where copy and original disagree on intact cords, the difference is most often one knot (21 of 70) or one digit in one place (8): copies were made place by place, knot by knot.
evidence: Zeros inside runs of equal neighbours: broken cords 18 of 21 have a value on the partner, intact cords 10 of 29 (one-sided Fisher p = 0.0003).

Differing matched values next to equal ones: one knot apart 21 against 1.4 when the differing values are shuffled between places (p < 0.001); one digit changed in one place 8 against 2.4 (p = 0.004); digits swapped 0; shifted by ×10 1.

levels.numbers: Lost values on broken cords reappear on the partner far more often than values at intact zeros; disagreements cluster at one knot or one digit.
levels.structure: Only places inside runs where both neighbours agree are counted, so the alignment is certain.
levels.reading: A copy was made by counting the knots of each place; a broken cord on one khipu can be restored from the other. Values that differ by more are probably separate records rather than slips.

knot_positions.title: Copies were knotted with the original at hand
knot_positions.summary: In linked copies the height of the units knots follows the original cord by cord: after removing the number of places, the knots above and the slow drift along the khipu, the positions still agree in 7 of 11 pairs (p < 0.01), for example AS175 → UR233 (0.81) and → UR232 (0.79), UR1114 ~ UR1123 (0.81). The slips in copies are ancient: the two modern records of the same khipus (KFG and OKR) disagree mostly by a whole place (×10, 123 of 344 differences), while copies disagree by single knots. Some khipus also repeat part of themselves: 7 khipus hold a run of at least four cords a second time, against 1–3 when their cords are shuffled — among them both HP055 and UR1084, and UR085, where 1498, 19, 73, 27 come back 113 cords later on cords of other colours.
evidence: Units height on matched equal cords (same number of places), corrected for places, knots above and an 11-cord running median: permutation p < 0.01 in 7 of 11 pairs — AS175 ~ UR233 0.81, AS175 ~ UR232 0.79, UR1114 ~ UR1123 0.81, UR267A ~ UR255 0.59, UR053C ~ UR053B 0.59, UR266 ~ UR275 0.46, HP055 ~ UR1084 0.44.
KFG against OKR records of the same khipus: 98.0% of values equal; of the differences 123 of 344 are shifts by a place (×10) and few are one-knot slips — the opposite of copies.
Internal repeats (a run of ≥ 4 cords with ≥ 3 different non-round values ≥ 10, repeated at a shift ≥ 2): 7 khipus against 1–3 in 10 shuffles.

The Inkawasi copies of sector C (UR255, UR256) re-lay their originals in a form of their own: every row has an empty cord between the gross amount and the fixed deduction (106, 0, 15; 1055, 0, 10 …), where the originals go straight on (106, 15, 91; 660, 10, 74); gross values of UR267A reappear on UR255 in 17 of 23 cases, the net values in only 9 of 22 — the reserved column for the net was never filled.

levels.numbers: Copies repeat the knot heights of the original, not only its numbers; modern records differ in another way (whole places).
levels.structure: Only matched cords with equal values and the same number of places are compared, after removing what the number itself explains.
levels.reading: Whoever knotted the copy had the original (or an exact model) beside them and followed it cord by cord. Single-knot slips between copies were made then, not by modern readers.

shares.title: Round amounts divided into equal shares
shares.summary: Runs of neighbouring cords that differ by exactly one and add up to a round number not divisible by their count are three times more common than chance: 100 as 33, 33, 34; 140 as 46, 47, 47; 2000 as 666, 667, 667 (24 runs against 8.3 for shifted sums, at most 21; sums of whole hundreds 6 against 0.5). UR190 (Huaca Pérez, Lima) repeats thirds of 100, 140 and 70 in the same places of groups 15–20; UR1161 (Ica) divides 100 into six (16, 16, 17, 17, 17, 17) beside 50 and 50; HP037 (Huacho) holds thirds of 400, 800, 2000 and 4000. The remainder always goes one by one to some of the shares — integer division done the same way at three places. More widely, group sums are whole hundreds about 2.4 times more often than expected even when their parts are not round, as if a set amount was spread out.
evidence: Runs of 2–6 cords in one group, all ≥ 10, differing by exactly 1, sum a multiple of 10 not divisible by the run length: 24 against a mean of 8.3 (max 21) when the sum is shifted by ±1…±5; multiples of 100: 6 against 0.5 (max 2).

Group sums that are multiples of 100, groups with ≥ 2 non-round cords and no total cord inside: 36 against 14.9 (max 26 of 20 shifts); for example UR015 5500 = 500 + 1782 + 1796 + 1422, UR275 4000, UR187 12,600, HP030 7200.
Not found in the 172 KFG khipus that are not in OKR (0 against 1.0) — the shares rest on three khipus.
Round-hundred group sums made of non-round parts do not replicate on the KFG-only khipus (6 against 1–11 for shifted sums).

levels.numbers: Equal shares with the remainder spread by ones; round group sums made of non-round parts.
levels.structure: Shares sit next to each other inside one group and, on UR190, in the same places of consecutive groups.
levels.reading: Some khipus record the division of a fixed amount among three or six — this is division, unlike the fractions p/q between groups, which were not found.

making.title: How khipus were made: cords cut to length, a local spacing, colours in passes
making.summary: Cords were cut to one length before knotting: a single knot takes about 0.54 cm of cord and each turn of a long knot 0.64 cm, and lengths with this taken back are more even in 311 of 392 khipus. The distance between places on a cord is a local habit: about 6.5 cm at Pachacamac, Inkawasi and Huaquerones, 7.5 cm at Ica, about 12 cm at Santa and Chancay; khipus of one site are more alike than with sites shuffled (p = 0.001), also after allowing for cord length and number of places and within one recording team. Inside a group, cords of one colour carry their units at a height of their own, as if each colour was knotted in a separate pass. Khipus with wrapped bundles (canutos) follow other rules (see that finding).
evidence: Knots shorten cords: within khipus, length against knots and turns −0.30; 0.54 cm per single knot, 0.64 cm per turn (18,751 cords). Length plus knot allowance: CV 0.159 against 0.180 measured and 0.172 with the allowance dealt out at random; more even in 311 of 392 khipus.

Median spacing between adjacent place clusters per khipu (202 khipus): within-site variance 2.89 against 3.95 with sites shuffled (p = 0.001); residuals after length and number of places p = 0.001; UR khipus only p = 0.001.
Height of the units cluster by cord colour, within groups and among cords with the same number of places: R² 0.165 against 0.100 with colours shuffled inside groups (max 0.122).

Cords of a group were cut as one batch: neighbouring cords differ in length by 8.9% within a group but by 12.8% across a group boundary, as much as random pairs (13.2%); on KFG-only khipus 12.4%, 16.7% and 17.4%.

levels.numbers: Knot size is measurable in the cord lengths.
levels.structure: Place spacing differs by site; colours within a group differ in knot height.
levels.reading: Cords were prepared to a set length and knotted to a local measure, colour by colour.

colours.title: Colour: a category inside a khipu, given new colours in copies
colours.summary: Within khipus light cords (W, AB, YB) carry larger numbers than dark ones (KB, MB, DB, B): in 119 of 211 khipus against 87 by chance (p = 0.002), and the same without total cords. In copies the matched cords rarely keep their colour (UR1114 ~ UR1123: 1 of 29), yet each colour of one khipu goes over to one colour of the other (375 of 548 cords against 287; 7 of 8 testable pairs when the colour blocks are kept and only shifted), also for pairs recorded by the same team. Colour marked a category consistently, but the copy gave it a colour of its own; there is no colour vocabulary shared by the khipus of one site. A warning for comparisons: recorders name colours differently — one khipu described by Ascher and by Urton agrees on 61 of 181 cords (Ascher's YB is Urton's AB).
evidence: Median value of light against dark cords within khipus: light larger in 119 of 211 against 87.0 with colours shuffled (p = 0.002); totals removed 114 of 203 against 83.8 (p = 0.002).

Copies: consistent colour mapping 375 of 548 matched cords against 286.6 (p = 0.003); circular shifts of the target colours p < 0.05 in UR1175 ~ UR233, UR1175 ~ UR232, UR266 ~ UR275, UR053C ~ UR053B, HP055 ~ UR1084, UR066 ~ UR067.
Colour order by value between khipus of one site: mean Spearman 0.077 against 0.002 (max 0.114) over 196 pairs — no shared vocabulary.
AS068 (Ascher) against UR281 (Urton), one object: colour equal on 61 of 181 matched cords; YB ↔ AB 56 times.
On the KFG-only khipus light cords are larger in 32 of 63 against 26.9 (p = 0.10): the same direction, not significant on its own.

Inside khipus colour marks a category with its own size of numbers: within groups (group means removed, colours shuffled only inside groups) colour explains values beyond chance in 52 of 162 khipus (1.6 expected), up to R² 0.93 on AS178; table columns keep one colour in 710 of 1716 cases (267 by chance), and such columns are more uniform in size (sd of log values 0.53 against 0.69). On UR1097 (Pachacamac) white cords with a short coloured top carry 1 under G0/BB tags and 5 under BG/VB/0D tags (R² 0.94).

Two-colour cords also keep to their own columns (slot agreement 8838 against 7686), without being larger. Single cords separating groups are mostly blank coloured markers (72% of coloured separators are empty) and are coloured unlike the head of the next group (same colour 188 of 763 against 347 for a random cord).

Two colours alternating along a group (period 2: 121 groups against 29 by chance) mark pairs of unlike entries: the two colours differ at least twofold in 9 of 17 strict cases (14% in other groups), e.g. UR1145 (Pachacamac) 5, 2, 4 beside 1000, 1100, 430; in UR1103, UR1150 and HP022 the two parts of a pair grow together.

levels.numbers: Large quantities sit on light cords more often than on dark ones.
levels.structure: In copies, colour groups map one to one although the colours themselves change.
levels.reading: Colour separated kinds of entries within a record; the meaning was kept in copying, the dye was not. Colours from different recorders need a translation table.

canutos.title: Canuto khipus: another system of long knots
canutos.summary: Eight khipus in the OKR database gather their pendants in bundles wrapped with coloured thread (canutos): UR039 (Huari), UR050 and UR054 (Soldi collection), UR052 (Banco Central de Reserva), UR055 (Museo Oro del Perú), UR110 and UR112 (Museo Temple Radicati) and UR144 (Pisco valley). They are exactly the khipus whose long knots keep nearly the same number of turns: among 120 khipus with at least 40 long knots they rank 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 9, 17 and 18 by the spread of turns (P ≈ 5·10⁻⁸; median sd 0.93 against 2.08). On them almost every cluster is a single long knot of 4–7 turns; the knots of one cord vary together, crowded cords have shorter knots and the lowest knot is often the shortest — the turns behave like a habit of the hand, not like decimal digits. They are also made differently: their pendants are camelid fibre (66%) or human hair (24%; UR055 entirely), while the rest of the corpus is cotton, and only they have cord ends wrapped with coloured thread. Bundles follow a standard: four cords (pairs on UR039, six on UR050), and the cords of a bundle look alike without being copies.
evidence: Turn sd per khipu (≥ 40 long knots): main mode 2.0–2.25 (73 khipus) and a separate cluster at 0.75–1.25 (12 khipus) holding 6 of the 8 canuto khipus; long knots make up 82–100% of the clusters on canuto khipus.

Turns on one cord correlate (UR055 0.34; UR052 0.38–0.58); knots per cord against turns per knot: UR144 −0.57, UR050, UR054 and UR055 about −0.3; the lowest knot is shorter on UR144 (38 of 42 cords), UR039 (23 of 26) and UR055 (101 of 147).

Bundle sizes: four cords in 23 of 24 bundles on UR144, 29 of 41 on UR055, 15 of 20 on UR112, 13 of 22 on UR110, 18 of 27 on UR052; six on UR050 (24 of 29); two on UR039 (41 of 45). Cords of one bundle share their number of clusters more often than random cords (UR112 0.75 against 0.45) but are identical in only 17–24%.

Fibre of pendants: canuto khipus camelid 0.66, human hair 0.24, cotton 0.10 (UR039 only); all other khipus cotton 0.53, unrecorded 0.45, camelid 0.009. Human-hair pendants: UR055 178, UR052 39, UR004 9. Wrapped ends (TT, 359 cords) only on UR055, UR050, UR112, UR052 and UR039.

All eight have long knots of one direction (S in the OKR records; decimal khipus 83 S against 100 Z), no subsidiaries and no knotless cords. A value signature from the KFG data finds no further canuto khipu among the 757. More widely, 51 of 611 OKR khipus (8%) show signs of non-decimal recording (long knots, figure-eights or spirals in upper places, or long knots of 10+ turns), twice as often among khipus without provenance (12%) as among those with a known site (6%).

Their knots stand 11.5–19 cm apart on a cord (median spacing of the other khipus: 7 cm), without a shared grid of heights; the cords of one bundle carry their top knot at a similar height (7 of 8 khipus), so a bundle was knotted together.

levels.numbers: Turn counts are bunched at 4–7 and do not behave like counted quantities.
levels.structure: Pendants in wrapped bundles, mostly of four; nearly every cluster is one long knot.
levels.reading: Canuto khipus are a separate kind of record (one of them from Huari); reading their knots as decimal numbers would be wrong. What the long knots stand for there is open.

counting.title: Almost-round counts were written as round
counting.summary: In numbers of two and three places the units 7, 8 and 9 are rarer than 1–6 (9 at 0.46 and 0.55 of their mean), in every recording team and at most sites, while numbers of four and five places have even units (9 at 0.84 and 1.24). And although smaller numbers are always the commoner ones, values one or two above a round number outnumber those one or two below it: 98–99 against 101–102 is 30 against 75, 198–199 against 201–202 is 10 against 28, 28–29 against 31–32 is 451 against 604. A count just short of a round number was recorded as the round number (or a target was met with a little to spare); the large numbers, sums of many counts, keep their full units.
evidence: Values ≥ 100 with non-zero units, relative to the mean of digits 1–6: 7 0.81, 8 0.87, 9 0.62; by recording team UR 0.63, AS 0.46, HP 0.69; by site Inkawasi 0.73, Pachacamac 0.63, Ica 0.28.
Units digit 9 by number of places: two 0.46, three 0.55, four 0.84, five 1.24 — the shortfall fades in large values, so it is not caused by crowded cords.
Endings 8–9 against 1–2 (values 20–999): 0.54 overall, below 1 at every site with enough data (Ica 0.35 … Inkawasi 0.72). It is not rounding to the nearest ten: digit 1 is not depleted (0.95).

Replicated on the 172 KFG khipus not in OKR: endings 8–9 against 1–2 are 376 against 569 (0.66). Khipus also differ in how much they round: 41 khipus have 60–100% round values (none expected from the corpus share), 98 have 0–10% (20 expected).

The surplus over round numbers also appears at thousands, where piece-by-piece counting is unlikely: within 20 of a whole thousand 16 values lie below and 36 above; within 5 of whole hundreds 149 below and 319 above. Part of the effect is therefore 'a target and a little more', not only rounding of small counts.

levels.numbers: Units 7–9 are scarce in small numbers, and values just below round numbers are missing.
levels.structure: The effect fades with the number of places and is shared by all recording teams.
levels.reading: Small amounts were counted with a habit of rounding up near a round number; totals made from them were added exactly.

forms.title: Tables prepared as forms, rows with a scale of their own
forms.summary: Many khipus are tables: groups of one size are rows and cord positions are columns. Empty cords stand in the same columns across rows more than by chance, and some tables have rows that were made but never filled: on UR1113 (between Ica and Pisco) six filled rows are followed by four rows of eleven cords with the same colour pattern (W W W W FR MB W W W W W) and no knots at all; 12 khipus have such blank rows, 38 in all. The rows are not equal allotments: against values shuffled within each column, rows are less even in 110 of 200 tables (10 expected) — a large row is large in every column, like a large community in a census. A fixed layout can also sit in the subsidiaries: UR093 (Museo Temple Radicati) and HP038 (Lima) give most pendants exactly eight subsidiaries.
evidence: 220 sets of equal-size groups: empty-slot agreement 12,002 against 11,436 when cords are shuffled within groups (max 11,488).

Blank rows (≥ 4 cords, no knots, colour pattern of a filled row of the same khipu): AS074 11, UR1057 5, UR1113 4, AS075 4, AS203 3, UR128 3 and six more khipus; they stand anywhere along the khipu (first third 8, middle 18, last third 12).
Row totals of 200 tables against values permuted within each column: less even in 110, more even in 4 (10 expected each).
Eight subsidiaries per pendant: UR093 on 90 pendants, HP038 on 24; the pendant equals the sum of its eight subsidiaries 19 times on UR093.
Replicated on KFG-only khipus: empty-slot agreement 3602 against 3491 (max 3513) in 65 sets.

Rows share one profile: within a table the same columns are large in every row (mean row-to-row Spearman 0.51, positive in 85% of 11,916 row pairs); the first column is the largest in 93 of 242 tables (47.5 expected), and zeros fall in the small columns (Spearman −0.27, negative in 145 tables against 55) — an empty slot means 'none'. Tables of one site share their column-size profile weakly (Spearman 0.15 against 0.02 elsewhere, p = 0.003).

A column also fixes how its entries are written: subsidiaries hang on the same columns from row to row (9100 against 8624 when shuffled within rows) and in the same number (8409 against 8057), and a column is either round or exact or single-digit throughout (12,341 against 11,474). Some columns were prepared and left almost empty in 80% of rows or more — 45 such columns, ten of them in two tables of UR006 (Leymebamba); they are coloured like the filled columns.

levels.numbers: Row totals differ more than the columns allow; blank rows hold no knots at all.
levels.structure: Colour patterns and empty slots repeat row by row; cords for rows were prepared in advance.
levels.reading: Khipu tables were laid out before they were filled, like a form with one line per unit (community, household, supplier).

subsidiaries.title: Subsidiaries are parts of the larger entries
subsidiaries.summary: Within khipus, pendants that carry subsidiaries hold larger numbers than those without (141 of 251 khipus against 108 by chance, p = 0.002). The subsidiaries usually add up to less than their pendant (2582 of 3846; median 27%), and they grow with it: within khipus the subsidiary sum rises with the pendant value (mean Spearman 0.24, positive in 131 of 176 khipus). They are not fixed fractions: once round numbers are set aside, exact halves, thirds, quarters and sixths are no commoner than near misses. Subsidiaries read like 'of which …' notes to the larger entries.
evidence: Median value of pendants with and without subsidiaries, within khipus: larger with subsidiaries in 141 of 251 against 107.6 with labels shuffled (p = 0.002).

Subsidiary sum against pendant (pendants ≥ 10 with subsidiaries): smaller 2582, equal 83, larger 639, empty 542; median ratio 0.27 (deciles 0.02–1.98). Within-khipu Spearman 0.243 against 0.000 shuffled.
Non-round pendants: subsidiary sum exactly 1/2 of the pendant 21 times against 18.5 for 1/2 of the pendant ± 1; 1/3 19 against 17; 1/4 20 against 18; 1/6 27 against 19.
Replicated on KFG-only khipus: mean Spearman (pendant, subsidiary sum) 0.32, positive in 52 of 64 khipus.

levels.numbers: Subsidiaries hang on large entries and scale with them, without a fixed fraction.
levels.structure: Most subsidiaries are smaller than their pendant.
levels.reading: A subsidiary specifies part of the entry it hangs from — 'of which so many'.

heads.title: A group opens with its largest entry
heads.summary: The first cord of a group is its largest about twice as often as chance: in 710 of 2529 groups against 375 expected, while the last cord is largest in only 334. The same holds on the 172 KFG khipus that are not in OKR (373 of 890 against 129). It is a local rule: the head comes first 3.3 times more often than chance at Inkawasi and 2–3 times at Ica and between Ica and Pisco, only 1.3 times at Pachacamac and Leymebamba, and never at Paracas (60 groups) or Santa (50). The head is rarely a total (21 cases equal the sum of the rest): it is the main entry, put before the smaller ones. Colour marks the edges of groups rather than the head: a colour found nowhere else in the group is carried by the first cord in 28% and by the last in 30% of groups, against 17% for cords in between. Single cords standing between groups are sometimes totals, mostly of the group that follows (9 of 94 against 1.7 when the sums are shifted).
evidence: Groups with ≥ 4 cords, ≥ 3 non-zero and a single maximum: first cord largest 710, last 334, expected Σ1/n = 375; heads equal to the sum of the rest 21. KFG-only khipus: 373 and 91 against 129.
Colour unique within the group: first cord 0.279 (3821 groups), cords in between 0.171, last cord 0.297.
Single-cord groups between groups of ≥ 3 cords (94): equal to the sum of the following group 9 (shifted sums 1.7), of the preceding one 4 (1.5), of both 1 (0.3).
By site, first cord largest against expected: Inkawasi 141 of 263 groups (3.33), between Ica and Pisco 3.12, Ica 2.09, Nazca 1.83, Pachacamac 1.29, Leymebamba 1.33, Ocucaje 0.32, Paracas 0, Santa 0.

Heads are a convention of the whole khipu: in 31 of 145 khipus 80–100% of groups have their largest cord first (none expected from group sizes); the heads of one khipu share a colour (0.84 against 0.56 for other cords), mostly white (W 0.56 against 0.30). Where there are no heads the order is reversed: within groups values rise at Leymebamba, Paracas, Santa and Ocucaje (mean ρ +0.11 to +0.15) and fall at Inkawasi, Arica and Ica (−0.15 to −0.18), all recorded by one team. Inkawasi summary khipus (UR278, UR270) lack heads while their detail khipus have them.
Leymebamba mirrors the rule: there the largest entry comes last (41 of 172 groups against 21 expected), and the last cords are often white or green (GG 0.16 against 0.05 for other cords).

levels.numbers: The largest value of a group tends to come first; it is seldom the sum of the others.
levels.structure: Colour brackets a group at both ends.
levels.reading: Groups were written from the main entry down — the chief item, community or category first.

Khipus 'between Ica and Pisco' reach Ber.text: Among them AS114, whose block recurs on AS123.

Berlin buys Gretzer's collection.text: About 40,000 objects, most labelled Pachacamac, among them UR212, AS131, AS170 and AS175.

The Ica khipus AS143, AS149, AS179 enter.text: One allocation spread over three khipus of the same batch.

Gaffron khipus in Detmold.text: Entered with other objects from his collection.

Basel buys khipus dug near Huacho.text: The ship's doctor Arnold Masarey sells a cache of cords; the museum's report calls them calendar records.

Nordenskiöld mounts the Huacho khipus.text: Ten fragments and loose cords are sewn onto a cloth, IVc.366.03, and pieces face both ways.

Nordenskiöld's calendar reading.title: Nordenskiöld's calendar reading
Nordenskiöld's calendar reading.text: He publishes the calendar hypothesis but not the Basel khipus.

The Aschers' Databooks.title: The Aschers' Databooks
The Aschers' Databooks.text: Cord-by-cord records of more than 200 khipus, with observations such as the 7 + 7 parts of AS131 and AS170.

Inkawasi storehouse excavated.title: Inkawasi storehouse excavated
Inkawasi storehouse excavated.text: Alejandro Chu recovers 34 khipus, some under chili peppers, peanuts and black beans.

Conklin khipus at Dumbarton Oaks.title: Conklin khipus at Dumbarton Oaks
Conklin khipus at Dumbarton Oaks.text: UR297 and UR298 enter the collection.

Huacones-Vilcahuasi.title: Huacones-Vilcahuasi
Huacones-Vilcahuasi.text: Eleven khipus found rolled together near a chili storeroom and a floor yupana.

Medrano traces the Basel khipus to Huach.title: Medrano traces the Basel khipus to Huacho
Medrano traces the Basel khipus to Huach.text: The museum archive names the burial ground near Huacho and the 1924 mounting.

This atlas.title: This atlas
This atlas.text: Corpus-wide search: every link between surviving khipus is a copy of one account.

Summary khipus.title: Summary khipus
Summary khipus.text: In the 2023 data no khipu records the group totals or column sums of another beyond chance (384 pairs against 415.6 on the offset baseline). The KFG release of October 2026 adds one exception, KH0697, which holds the section totals of AS109 (see the findings).

Compilations.title: Compilations
Compilations.text: Apart from the Basel fragments, no khipu combines runs from two or more other khipus.

Colonial documents.title: Colonial documents
Colonial documents.text: About 2,300 numbers from roughly 70 open transcriptions match no digitized khipu.

Huacones-Vilcahuasi hierarchy.title: Huacones-Vilcahuasi hierarchy
Huacones-Vilcahuasi hierarchy.text: Totals of one khipu on the next are at the level of chance (offset baseline).

Opposite attachment in copies.title: Opposite attachment in copies
Opposite attachment in copies.text: Recto on one copy and verso on the other in 7 of 10 pairs, against 50% at random (p ≈ 0.17).

Same suppliers in the same order.title: Same suppliers in the same order
Same suppliers in the same order.text: Deposit sizes of different Inkawasi khipus do not correlate by position.

Copies respect group boundaries.title: Copies respect group boundaries
Copies respect group boundaries.text: Run endpoints fall on group boundaries in 38% of cases against 46% expected.

Broken cords as lower bounds.title: Broken cords as lower bounds
Broken cords as lower bounds.text: Sums with a broken part are exact half as often (35% vs 68%), but the sign shows no loss of knots.

Equal-share convention.title: Equal-share convention
Equal-share convention.text: Pairs of equal-total groups are not over-represented corpus-wide (p ≈ 0.1).

Pachacamac style vs Huacho style.title: Pachacamac style vs Huacho style
Pachacamac style vs Huacho style.text: Simple numeric features do not separate site-museum Pachacamac khipus from Huacho khipus.

Sign convention.title: Sign convention
Sign convention.text: Neither attachment side nor colour marks negative cords.

Syllables in non-decimal khipus.title: Syllables in non-decimal khipus
Syllables in non-decimal khipus.text: The non-decimal signs of Wari-style khipus have far too small an alphabet for syllables.

Calendar reading.title: Calendar reading
Calendar reading.text: Group and cord counts give no calendar numbers beyond chance.

Colour of the product.title: Colour of the product
Colour of the product.text: Colour is not carried into copies and does not mark the product at Inkawasi.

Ordered totals and strided copies.title: Ordered totals and strided copies
Ordered totals and strided copies.text: Group totals of one khipu repeated in the same order on another (192 khipus with at least three non-round totals ≥ 100): every pair above the shifted-value baseline is a copy already known or a second recording of one object. Within Inkawasi, every p-th record of one khipu laid against consecutive records of another (strides 2–8): only UR269 ~ UR275 stands out; the rest is at the level expected from the number of strides and offsets tried.

Place-dependent constants and small-valu.title: Place-dependent constants and small-valued copies
Place-dependent constants and small-valu.text: A value fixed by the place of the record in its block, as on UR269, was sought on every khipu and every cord position (blocks between separator groups; records shuffled within blocks): UR269 is the only clear case (p ≈ 0.003; next UR037, p ≈ 0.05 on values of 2 and 4). Identical groups of six or more small values (< 100) on khipus with different museum numbers: every rare match is a second recording of one object or AS003 ~ AS215; the rest are uniform runs such as seven 10s.

A hidden network.title: A hidden network
A hidden network.text: Every pair of the 757 khipus (286,146 pairs) was scored for shared rare values (≥ 100, not multiples of 10) and for a group total of one standing on a cord of the other. Beyond the known links, second recordings of one object under two numbers and one new link (AS104 ~ UR234), the excess over shifted values is spread thinly over thousands of pairs, and khipus from one place share no more rare values than random khipus of the same size (place labels shuffled: p = 0.075). The known links are small separate groups, not parts of one structure.

Knot direction and attachment side in co.title: Knot direction and attachment side in copies
Knot direction and attachment side in co.text: On cords that two linked khipus share, the copy does not follow the original's knot direction beyond what khipus of the same place share anyway (long knots are reversed on about half of the copies), nor its attachment side (recto or verso of a whole khipu follows how bundles were laid out: both members of a two-khipu bundle are always opposite). Colour is kept more often than chance (26% against 16%). Cords attached on the other side within a khipu mark sections — whole groups at the start or end, knotless separators — and are not copied.

Operations beyond addition.title: Operations beyond addition
Operations beyond addition.text: Fractions (one group equal to another times p/q with rounding, q = 2–12), products (a × b = c within a group), squares and cubes, and a circle's area (π·r² or 3·r²) were sought in every khipu. Against values shifted by 1–5, with each value combination counted once and round numbers left out: fractions 7 against 11.9, products 228 against 217, powers 167 against 142, circle 188 against 245 — none above chance. Besides sums, only whole-number multiples (×8 on UR271, halving on AS026B) and proportional shares (the Berlin ninths) occur.

Breakdown tables outside Inkawasi.title: Breakdown tables outside Inkawasi
Breakdown tables outside Inkawasi.text: Group totals of one khipu that reappear, in order, as the first cords of another khipu's groups (the Inkawasi nine-part tables) were sought in the whole corpus: pairs with four or more such totals number 4 against 0.5 with shifted values, and all four are Inkawasi pairs already known. Outside Inkawasi nothing stands above the baseline.

Colour of total cords.title: Colour of total cords
Colour of total cords.text: A cord equal to the sum of the others in its group has a colour of its own more often than chance (56 of 134 against 39), but the excess comes from the Inkawasi peanut ledgers (white gross cords) and UR297; elsewhere 16 of 50 against 13.2 (p = 0.16). Marking the total by colour is a local habit, not a general rule.

Formats and find-places.title: Formats and find-places
Formats and find-places.text: Khipus that repeat the same unit of group sizes (for example six cords and a separator) come from the same place no more often than chance (19% of pairs against 11%, p = 0.20; 22 khipus with a known place). Column profiles that look alike point to the same place only weakly (20% against 8%, p = 0.06), although they do find second recordings and known links.

Calendar, ceque and lunar numbers.title: Calendar, ceque and lunar numbers
Calendar, ceque and lunar numbers.text: 365, 360, 354, 328 (shrines of the ceque system) and 41 (ceque lines) occur no more often than their neighbouring numbers; neighbouring cords of 29 and 30 (alternating months) are as rare as 28/29 or 30/31; groups per khipu do not peak at 12, 24, 30 or 36, and no khipu has 360 or 365 pendants.

Number curiosities.title: Number curiosities
Number curiosities.text: Golden-ratio neighbours (1.618 ± 1%: 67 against 70–179 for nearby ratios), squares (95 against 80–150 for shifted values), triangular numbers, primes, arithmetic progressions of four cords, doubling runs (x, 2x, 4x) and multiples of 9 are all at the level of their baselines.

Check digits, running and grand totals.title: Check digits, running and grand totals
Check digits, running and grand totals.text: No first or last cord of a group equals the sum of the others modulo 9 or 10 beyond chance (244 against 257); no cord equals the sum of all the cords before it in its group (11 against 17.5); no cord holds the total of the whole khipu (2 khipus against 1–3); the difference between the totals of neighbouring groups is not written down (0.173 against 0.163–0.175 for groups further apart).

Mirror copies.title: Mirror copies
Mirror copies.text: No khipu copies another read from the other end: runs of five informative values shared in reverse are as many as forward ones and come only from repetitive runs, while every known copy runs forward.

Threes and half-units.title: Threes and half-units
Threes and half-units.text: Group sizes 3, 6, 9 and 12 are not preferred over 4, 5 and 10 when each khipu is counted once; 50, 500 and 5000 are not more frequent than 40 and 60, 400 and 600 — only 100 and 1000 stand out.

Cords that count cords.title: Cords that count cords
Cords that count cords.text: No cord gives the number of cords of its group or of the khipu more often than that number ± 1–3, and no runs number the cords (v, v + 1, v + 2, v + 3: 4 against 2.4 for shuffled cords).

Benford's law and counting in pairs.title: Benford's law and counting in pairs
Benford's law and counting in pairs.text: First digits do not follow Benford's law anywhere (43% ones against 30%: values sit just above powers of ten), and no khipus count in pairs: khipus with at least 80% even non-round values are 2 against 0.2 expected, one of them because of repeats.

Fixed rates and simple fractions.title: Fixed rates and simple fractions
Fixed rates and simple fractions.text: Two columns of a table do not stand in a fixed integer ratio row by row beyond what round numbers produce (exact multiples against multiples ± 1 are 2.35 to 1 in the same row and 2.32 to 1 between neighbouring rows), and subsidiaries are not fixed halves, thirds or tenths of their pendants once round numbers are set aside.

Header codes and hidden bases.title: Header codes and hidden bases
Header codes and hidden bases.text: The first group of a khipu does not recur as a place code on other khipus of the same site (1 shared sequence, as at other positions), and khipus that never use a digit above 5 or 6 are khipus of small counts or canuto khipus, not records in another base.

Moieties, ranked lists and pairs.title: Moieties, ranked lists and pairs
Moieties, ranked lists and pairs.text: Groups do not come in pairs of halves (1–2, 3–4 tighter in 147 of 316 khipus, 2–3, 4–5 in 167), are not ranked lists once the large first cord is set aside (11 strictly descending groups against 7.1), and neighbouring cords do not form male–female pairs.

Plans and facts; rounding in copies.title: Plans and facts; rounding in copies
Plans and facts; rounding in copies.text: No rounded khipu repeats another khipu's values rounded to tens (74 pairs above all shuffles against about 150 expected); copies were not rounded, and they do not repeat the original's cord lengths once the knots' use of length is removed.
